This can also be understood as referring generally to the distant preparatory stages (*dūramgamā-prayoga*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in all three vehicles, wherein one practices the study of the truths by contemplating the four truths,
as well as the non-conceptual contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, the ancient sūtras and śāstras all state that the practitioners of the three vehicles equally contemplate the four truths to enter the noble path (*ārya-mārga*).
Just as with the contemplation on the truth of suffering,
so too is the non-conceptual contemplation regarding the other two truths.
This illustrates the mode of practice for the preparatory means.
Previously, during the preparatory stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one relied on conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) to contemplate the various perceptions and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of suffering and so forth.
Now, upon entering the path of seeing, these general characteristics are all eliminated, and conceptual proliferation is cut off.
If the two vehicles turn toward the signless True Suchness as manifested solely by the meaning of the selflessness of persons,
whereas according to the Mahāyāna, they turn toward the signless True Suchness as manifested by both forms of selflessness.
The Abhidharma also states that within the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) within one's own continuum,
supramundane wisdom arises through the direct realization of its suchness (tathatā),
thereby permanently severing all twenty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
This text explains that the two vehicles observe suchness (*tathatā*) to sever afflictions. Tái says:
"Since they have attained liberation from all general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) within the truths previously observed by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)."
Therefore, one should know that when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one takes the path of seeing as its collective object.
Because the four truths previously observed by conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) serve as the means for realizing the equality of emptiness,
one enters the path of seeing.
When one subsequently emerges from the contemplation of emptiness and again contemplates the truths,
this constitutes the sixteenfold contemplation of the truths.
Next, the second question is answered.
Regarding the statement, "The establishment of the path of seeing is by way of two principles," etc.,
Bukei (Supplementer) states:
"The meaning of the answer is twofold."
First, regarding the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is the drawing forth of learners through signless equality,
wherein nine moments of mind are distinguished by means of signs;
second, there is the establishment of a single moment of mind.
This clearly elucidates the true realization of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Thus, at the time of the first reliance (*āśraya*), there are nine moments of mind;
as for the subsequent reliance during the practice (*caryā*):
Regarding the statement, "There is only a single mind;

it is based on the superior power established by the first [moment]," this means that the wisdom of realization in a single thought-moment contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four truths within the three realms as a whole.
This is called the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*). It consists of four moments of mind,
which are the self-evident aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of that very non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), transformed so as to take itself as its object.
It is called the fourfold subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
It is the samādhi associated with realized knowledge (*adhigama-jñāna*), characterized by śamatha;
it is the ninth moment of mind.
Alternatively, one may provisionally establish the nine mental states based on non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) across two moments of thought:
the first moment establishes the four patiences regarding the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*),
and the second moment establishes the four cognitions regarding the dharma (*dharmanirjñāna*).
Whether it be patience (*kṣānti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), both take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object;
therefore, these are collectively combined into the category of the four dharmas of knowledge.
There are four minds.
That is to say, the preceding forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) each possess a self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that reflects back upon its own essence;
these taken together are collectively termed "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*).
This category likewise comprises four moments of mind.
If one opens up the patience and knowledge, there are sixteen moments of mind,
established according to the Buddha’s voice.
These consist of the two moments of the patience of the dharma of suffering and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering.
In a single moment, one abandons the lower afflictions that cause suffering;
because this involves the definitive discernment of the phenomena of suffering, it is ultimately designated as "one mind.

This continues up to the establishment of the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
Having severed the afflictions pertaining to the Truth of the Path and having fully discerned the ultimate nature of the Truth of the Path,
the period during which this occurs is termed the "single-mindedness of the Path."
The Tripiṭaka Master further states:
"This sixteen-moment contemplation of the path of insight (darśanamārga) is established based on the four divisions of the true path of insight (bhūta-darśanamārga)."
Just as in the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four truths is taken as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*);

so too, in the subsequent path of seeing (*anvayamārga*), the four patiences (*kṣānti*) and four knowledges (*jñāna*) take the suchness of the four truths of the three realms as their objective aspect.
Just as in the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) reflexively illuminates itself,

so too in the subsequent path of seeing (*anvayadarśanamārga*), the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) take the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) as their object and illuminate it through their own transformation.

Thus, within these nine moments of mind, the preceding eight are further distinguished as sixteen moments of mind, because within each category there are both *kṣānti* (patience) and *jñāna* (knowledge).
As for the statement that "there is one moment of mind" due to the establishment of the third [category] through its predominant power: [End of segment]
This means that immediately upon the sudden severance of the afflictions of the path of seeing, the wisdom of the ultimate *tathatā* (suchness) arises;
simultaneously, there is also the path of *śamatha*, which is the path of seeing according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The *Abhidharmapitaka* (Jñānaprasthāna), fascicle nine, also states:
"Furthermore, as previously explained, the distinctions of the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are all conventionally established;
they are not [ultimately] real."
Why is this? Because within the supramundane state, there is individual internal realization,
which is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Tai says:
Because the mind arises due to the causal conditions of meditative concentration,
it is called "the mind that is manifested."
The eight types of *śamatha* are explained separately because they involve distinct observations;
the eight types of *vipaśyanā* are distinguished because they cause the mind to abide in a state of uniform quiescence within the same object.
Question: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are sixteen moments of mind in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
The preceding text of this treatise also states:
"In each of the upper and lower truths, there are two moments of mind;
these likewise constitute sixteen moments of mind."
This refers to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
For what reason does this text state that the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) consists of only nine moments of mind?
Furthermore, the preceding treatise states:
The Path of Seeing is called the path of union because concentration and wisdom proceed together.
Why, then, does this text first mention wisdom and subsequently the eight concentrations?
To answer: according to the actual principle, [it is as follows].
Concentration and wisdom are always conjoined.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, patience (*kṣānti*) is also called wisdom (*jñāna*);
when the eight truths are known, because the function of patience—consisting of aspiration, seeking, and observation—increases, patience is termed *śamatha*.
These are called the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
The eight knowledges are identical to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*).
Knowledge is the aspiration for the mental state of tranquil concentration; its function of increasing [calm] is designated as *śamatha*.
These are the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
The eight knowledges also differ from the sixteen moments of mind;
however, in this particular text, the sense of seeking observation through the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) is predominant.
The eight knowledges previously mentioned are called *vipaśyanā*.
That which subsequently arises with the eight knowledges, characterized by aspiration, mental one-pointedness, and a powerful function of tranquility,
is called *śamatha*.
The meaning of "quiescence" is identical;
they are collectively described as the single mind.
It is only because of differences in expansion and contraction that their designations differ.
Regarding its essential nature,
it is no different from other texts in stating that it consists of the eight patiences and the eight knowledges.
Furthermore, a Western master offers another interpretation, saying:
The Path of Vision (darśanamārga) does not actually sever the afflictions;
rather, various different explanations are given according to different capacities.
Some say it is severed through the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Some say that it is severed through the contemplation of the sixteen truths,
while others say it is severed through the nine mental states;
at the time of the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one realizes *tathatā* in a continuous succession.
This is called the ultimate path of true seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It should be understood that there is also initial wisdom followed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
just as in the previously described path of semblance seeing (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Since it is similar to the previously explained knowledge (*jñāna*),
the subsequent term "concentration" (*samādhi*) may also be applied; thus,
within the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is a single dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*).
Regarding the two moments of dharma-knowledge and the two minds,
Master Ji says:
"Briefly, there are two explanations."
Regarding the phrase "the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) and so forth":
the word *pakṣa* means "category" (*prakāra*). As for the term "category," it refers to a class or type.
This includes the patience of receptivity (*kṣānti*).
These four types of patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*),
together with the single category of the knowledge of the Dharma (*dharmajñāna*), are collectively termed the "four minds."
Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is also like this.
These constitute the category of knowledge (*jñāna-skandha*), which consists of eight [knowledges] capable of performing the function of abandoning afflictions.
The category of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) consists of eight, because they enable the mind to abide in tranquility.
Taken collectively, they are designated as one;
thus, it is said there are nine minds.
This is because the category of concentration lacks the efficacy of severing afflictions and is therefore not considered wisdom.
However, they are collectively termed "one mind.
Although wisdom exists during the time of concentration and concentration exists during the time of wisdom,
their functional capacities are distinct.
It is not discussed whether wisdom is obscured during the time of meditative concentration, or concentration is obscured during the time of wisdom.
Regarding what is called the "category of dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) in the two explanations:
One does not take its dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) as the object;
rather, one takes its dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti), because this patience belongs to the category of dharma-knowledge.
This dharma-patience is fourfold.
The types of patience (*kṣānti*) constitute four [moments];
thus, there are eight mental states.
These are able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and are therefore the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Therefore, it receives the name "knowledge.
The four dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*), combined into a single mind,
are called the path of pure *śamatha*.
Because they cannot sever afflictions and are therefore not paths of uninterrupted transition,
these are collectively termed the "nine minds.
According to one interpretation, the four consist of the receptivities and knowledges regarding the dharma.
The types of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) constitute four moments of mind;
these are called the "eight minds.
This is because they are practiced in conjunction during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
These eight possess a category of concentration simultaneously;
because they cannot sever the afflictions,
they collectively constitute a single state of mind.
Wisdom constitutes eight minds;
thus, there are nine in total.

In the sixth interpretation of the sutra, there are seven phrases regarding the synonyms for afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the statement that "the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa) are called 'turtles' because they resemble the five limbs [of a turtle]," Tai says:
"The five hindrances possess the sense of concealment."
The single category of the tail is excluded because it serves no purpose.
Ji says:
The tortoise shell has five uses,
which are called the five similar branches.
Second, its anger is like that of a female camel.
A female camel harbors ill will toward the grass she grazes upon;
likewise, anger arises from directing ill will toward others.
Third, stinginess and envy are like congealed blood.
Because congealed blood is thin, weak, and lacks substance,
so too are gains and offerings.
The four types of sensory desires, such as form and so forth, are like meat on a butcher’s block.
When not specifically assigned to a subject, it arises above [the preceding term] to indicate an obstacle to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
The fifth, ignorance (*avidyā*), is called "the wolf's greed.
Jing says:
In the Western Regions there is an insect whose form is as large as a jackal and which is extremely dull-witted.
Because the old name for it in the *Vibhāṣā* was incorrect, it was said that there is a snake named Māndhaka.
Being blind oneself, one gives birth to a child who is also blind,
and causes others to become blind in the places where they are terrified.
Tai said: "The 'rat-fox' (*mǔláng*) is fond of fame.
The rat-fox has many tails;
when a snake wishes to strike it, it uses its tail to block the snake's mouth."
Just as a snake cannot bite [if it is restrained],
so too does ignorance obstruct hearing and knowledge,
such that one is unable to hear the Dharma.
Tài preserves both interpretations.
Furthermore, he states:
"In the Western Regions, they are called 'Ear-hair People' (Karṇaprāvaraṇa)."
The ear canals have hair that obstructs sound so one cannot hear the voices of people;
these six doubts are like a forked road.
The seventh is the conceit of "I am" (asmimāna), which is called the Cakravāḍa mountain.
Because this conceit of "I am" obstructs the pursuit of transcendence,
it is as difficult to cross over as the Cakravāḍa mountains.
The seventh [section] explains the three— greed, hatred, and delusion—
as unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) by virtue of their capacity to incite karma.
